title: Services
scopeHtml: Scope: Service types and lifecycle, onStartCommand semantics, foreground services and their rules, bound services, background-start restrictions, FGS types per release, priority effects, and Service vs WorkManager. Version-specific FGS facts are marked "verify" where behavior has shifted between releases.

notes.title: Started, bound and both
notes.html:
The idea. A Service is an Android component with no screen, for work that should continue when no Activity is visible. There are two ways to use it, and they differ in who controls its life.

  • Started service: someone calls startService() / startForegroundService(). It keeps running until it stops itself (stopSelf()) or someone calls stopService(). Lifecycle: onCreate -> onStartCommand (each start) -> onDestroy.
  • Bound service: clients call bindService() and talk to it through an IBinder. It lives while at least one client is bound. Lifecycle: onCreate -> onBind (first client) -> onUnbind (last client leaves) -> onDestroy.
  • Both: a service can be started and bound. It then stays alive until it is both stopped and has no clients. Music players do this: start so music continues after the UI leaves, bind so the UI can control it.
startService  ──► onCreate ─► onStartCommand ─► (running) ─► stopSelf ─► onDestroy
bindService   ──► onCreate ─► onBind ─► (clients) ─► last unbind ─► onUnbind ─► onDestroy
both: destroyed only when stopped AND no binders remain

Details: onCreate runs once per instance; onStartCommand runs for every start; onBind is called once for the first bind (the same IBinder is cached for later clients unless onRebind is used after onUnbind returns true). Service is a singleton per process; a second startService does not create a second instance.

Real products. Spotify and YouTube Music use a started foreground service (so playback survives) plus a MediaBrowserService/MediaSession binding for controllers (Android Auto, Wear OS, notification); Google Maps navigation similarly.

Analogy. A started service is a night guard you hire until you fire him. A bound service is a taxi that stays while a passenger is inside. A guard who also lets people ask him questions is both.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing startService called twice creates two instances.
  • Thinking a bound service stops when you call stopService; it stays until clients unbind.
  • Forgetting a service is destroyed only when both conditions (stopped and unbound) hold.

notes.title: Service threading
notes.html:
The idea. A Service does not run on its own thread or process. All its callbacks (onCreate, onStartCommand, onBind) run on the main thread of the app, unless you declare android:process. Blocking there causes ANRs (20 s for foreground service start callbacks, about 200 s for background services; confirm in docs).

class SyncService : Service() {
    private val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.IO)
    override fun onStartCommand(i: Intent?, f: Int, id: Int): Int {
        scope.launch { doSync(); stopSelf(id) }       // off the main thread
        return START_NOT_STICKY
    }
    override fun onDestroy() { scope.cancel(); super.onDestroy() }
    override fun onBind(i: Intent?): IBinder? = null
}

Options for background work: coroutines on Dispatchers.IO (cancel in onDestroy), executors, HandlerThread (what IntentService did), or LifecycleService + lifecycleScope. Binder calls from other processes arrive on Binder threads (a pool of up to 16 per process), not the main thread, so AIDL implementations must be thread-safe.

Real products. Upload services (Google Photos, WhatsApp media upload) run coroutines/OkHttp on IO inside a foreground service; they never do network on the main thread.

Analogy. A service is a job description, not an extra employee. The work still lands on the owner's desk (main thread) unless he hires a helper.

Common interview traps.

  • Assuming Service means "background thread".
  • Forgetting AIDL methods run on Binder threads (concurrency bugs).
  • Not cancelling the scope in onDestroy, leaking work.

notes.title: onStartCommand return values and restart semantics
notes.html:
The idea. If the system kills your service (low memory), onStartCommand's return value tells it what to do afterwards.

Return Behaviour after kill
START_NOT_STICKY Do not recreate unless there are pending start intents. Best for work you can lose or re-request
START_STICKY Recreate the service, call onStartCommand with null intent (so state must come from storage)
START_REDELIVER_INTENT Recreate and redeliver the last intent (and pending ones) until stopSelf(startId) is called; used for must-finish tasks
START_STICKY_COMPATIBILITY Legacy; no guarantee

Restart is not immediate: the system schedules it with an exponential backoff (starting around 1 second and growing, up to about 1 hour; confirm values). On Android 8+ restarting a background service may be refused by background-start limits, and after force-stop a service is never restarted until the user opens the app.

Spot-the-bug.

override fun onStartCommand(i: Intent?, f: Int, id: Int): Int {
    val url = i!!.getStringExtra("url")      // NPE after START_STICKY restart: i is null
    download(url); return START_STICKY
}

Fix: handle null (i ?: return START_NOT_STICKY, or read persisted state), or choose START_REDELIVER_INTENT. Also stopSelf(startId) with the correct id prevents stopping while a newer start request is queued.

Real products. Download managers (Play Store updates) use redeliver semantics via persisted queues; music players use sticky with saved queue state.

Analogy. If a shop assistant faints mid-job, NOT_STICKY says "forget it", STICKY says "someone new, figure out where we were", REDELIVER says "someone new, here is the same order slip again".

Common interview traps.

  • Not handling a null intent after START_STICKY.
  • Expecting restart after force-stop or when the user swipes with stopWithTask.
  • Believing STICKY gives instant revival; it uses backoff.

notes.title: stopSelf, stopService and destroy
notes.html:
The idea. A started service never stops by itself. Someone must say stop.

  • stopSelf() stops the service now. stopSelf(startId) stops only if startId is the latest start request; so an older request finishing does not kill a newer one still being processed.
  • stopService(intent) is the same from outside.
  • stopForeground(STOP_FOREGROUND_REMOVE or STOP_FOREGROUND_DETACH) drops foreground status (keeps service) and removes or keeps the notification.
  • If clients are still bound, onDestroy is delayed until they unbind.
  • After onDestroy, do not touch the instance: scopes should already be cancelled, receivers unregistered, binders released.
scope.launch {
    work()
    stopSelf(startId)        // safe with multiple queued starts
}

IntentService did this automatically after its queue was empty; hand-written services often forget and leak (a service never stopped appears in Settings > Running services and burns battery; watchdogs may report it).

Real products. Upload and sync services stop themselves on empty queue; analytics services use stopSelf with counters.

Analogy. Switching off the lights when the last person leaves; startId is checking nobody new walked in while you were reaching for the switch.

Common interview traps.

  • Using stopSelf() instead of stopSelf(startId) with concurrent starts.
  • Calling stopService and expecting destruction while still bound.
  • Forgetting to clean up in onDestroy.

notes.title: Foreground service, the notification and the 5-second rule
notes.html:
The idea. A foreground service is a started service that tells the user "I'm working" with a notification. In return Android treats it as high priority (process importance foreground-ish) and gives it more freedom.

How.

// Caller (from foreground, or an allowed exemption)
ContextCompat.startForegroundService(ctx, Intent(ctx, TrackService::class.java))

// In the Service, within ~5 seconds
override fun onStartCommand(i: Intent?, f: Int, id: Int): Int {
    val n = NotificationCompat.Builder(this, "track")
        .setSmallIcon(R.drawable.ic_nav).setContentTitle("Trip in progress").build()
    ServiceCompat.startForeground(this, 1, n, ServiceInfo.FOREGROUND_SERVICE_TYPE_LOCATION)
    return START_NOT_STICKY
}

The 5-second rule (production incident). From API 26, after startForegroundService() the service must call startForeground() within about 5 seconds or the system throws ForegroundServiceDidNotStartInTimeException ("Context.startForegroundService() did not then call Service.startForeground()"), crashing the app. Common causes: a heavy Application.onCreate/DI init delaying the service; slow main thread at boot; stopSelf() called before startForeground (still must call it); notification channel not created (on API 26+ a missing channel makes the notification invalid and can crash with Bad notification for startForeground); starting the service from a path that then calls stopService quickly. Fix: call startForeground as the first thing in onCreate/onStartCommand, use a prebuilt channel, keep init light, and for Android 12+ use ForegroundServiceStartNotAllowedException handling.

Notification behaviour across releases.

  • Android 8 (API 26): a notification channel is mandatory.
  • Android 12 (API 31): notifications from foreground services can be delayed up to 10 seconds unless the service is marked immediate (FOREGROUND_SERVICE_IMMEDIATE behaviour via setForegroundServiceBehavior), exempt cases being media, calls, etc.
  • Android 13 (API 33): POST_NOTIFICATIONS runtime permission; if denied, the service still runs as foreground but the notification is not shown, though it still appears in the Task Manager ("Active apps").
  • Android 14 (API 34): the user can swipe away a foreground service notification (except for some types like media, calls, device policy); the service keeps running, and the Task Manager entry stays.
  • Always confirm per-version details in the official foreground service docs.

Real products. Uber driver, Google Maps, Strava, Spotify, and Zoom calls all show persistent notifications; Android shows a "Foreground services" list in Task Manager since Android 13.

Analogy. A construction crew must put up a "Work in progress" sign within five minutes of starting or the city shuts the site.

Common interview traps.

  • Starting the foreground service from the background on API 31+ without an exemption.
  • Missing startForeground call when stopping early.
  • Assuming notification permission denial stops the service.

notes.title: Local bound service via Binder, Messenger and AIDL
notes.html:
The idea. To call methods on a service from an Activity, you bind and receive an IBinder. How you build that binder depends on whether client and service are in the same process.

Mechanism Same process Cross-process Threading Use
Local Binder subclass yes no calls run on caller thread App-internal: Activity controls a service
Messenger (wraps a Handler) yes yes messages serialised on the Handler's thread Simple IPC, one-way commands, no concurrency
AIDL yes yes calls on Binder threads, concurrent Typed API, multiple clients, high throughput 
class PlayerService : Service() {
    inner class LocalBinder : Binder() { fun get(): PlayerService = this@PlayerService }
    private val binder = LocalBinder()
    override fun onBind(i: Intent?): IBinder = binder
}
// Client
private val conn = object : ServiceConnection {
    override fun onServiceConnected(n: ComponentName, b: IBinder) { svc = (b as PlayerService.LocalBinder).get() }
    override fun onServiceDisconnected(n: ComponentName) { svc = null }   // process died; connection stays valid
}
bindService(Intent(this, PlayerService::class.java), conn, BIND_AUTO_CREATE)
// onStop: unbindService(conn)

Binder transaction details: the data limit is about 1 MB per process shared across all in-flight transactions (TransactionTooLargeException); AIDL parcels must be small, use files/ContentProvider for big data. Death notification via linkToDeath/onServiceDisconnected and onBindingDied tells you the other process died.

Bound service leak (spot-the-bug). Calling bindService in onCreate with no matching unbindService, or binding with the Application context from an Activity and keeping a ServiceConnection inner class: logcat shows Activity has leaked ServiceConnection ... that was originally bound here, and the service never dies because the binding persists. Pair binds with unbinds in matching lifecycle methods (onStart/onStop), and never call unbindService twice (IllegalArgumentException: Service not registered).

Real products. MediaBrowserServiceCompat (Android Auto, Spotify), Google Play Services' AIDL APIs, and Android's own system services are all AIDL/Binder. Messenger is common in older SDKs for simple cross-process commands.

Analogy. Local Binder: the receptionist hands you a direct internal phone. Messenger: you drop letters in an inbox read one by one. AIDL: a switchboard with many lines handling several callers at once.

Common interview traps.

  • Using a local Binder for cross-process calls (ClassCastException).
  • Passing large data through Binder (1 MB cap).
  • Treating AIDL calls as main-thread safe; they come in on pool threads.

notes.title: Background start restrictions (API 26 and later)
notes.html:
The idea. To protect battery, Android 8.0 (API 26) stopped apps from starting plain services when they are in the background. If your app is not visible, startService() throws IllegalStateException: Not allowed to start service Intent ...: app is in background.

Rules.

  • An app is "in the foreground" if it has a visible Activity, a foreground service, or something bound from a foreground app. After you go background there is a grace period of a few minutes (about 1 minute on API 26, shorter later) where starting a service is still allowed.
  • From the background you should use startForegroundService() (and call startForeground quickly), but Android 12 (API 31) further blocked this too: it throws ForegroundServiceStartNotAllowedException unless an exemption applies (high-priority FCM message, exact-alarm callback, notification action tap, SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW, BOOT_COMPLETED for certain types, user-visible task, WorkManager expedited jobs, etc.). Android 14 adds more type-specific rules and Android 15 restricts BOOT_COMPLETED for certain types.
  • For deferred work prefer WorkManager/JobScheduler, which the system runs when appropriate.

Production incident. A push notification (data message) handler calls startService to download content. Works in testing, fails for users who haven't opened the app in a day: crash IllegalStateException ... app is in background or ForegroundServiceStartNotAllowedException appears on Android 12+. Fix: use a high-priority FCM message (which grants a short foreground-start exemption), or enqueue expedited WorkManager work, and wrap startForegroundService in try/catch with a fallback.

Real products. Slack, WhatsApp and Gmail handle incoming FCM by doing quick work in onMessageReceived or scheduling expedited work, instead of starting plain services.

Analogy. A shop closing for the night: once the front door is locked, you can no longer wave in a new delivery truck; you have to book it for tomorrow with the manager (WorkManager).

Common interview traps.

  • Claiming startForegroundService works from anywhere on API 31+.
  • Forgetting to catch ForegroundServiceStartNotAllowedException.
  • Thinking the restriction applies to bound services too (binding from a background app is allowed, though it won't start it in the background in all cases).

notes.title: IntentService deprecation and migration
notes.html:
The idea. IntentService was a convenience: a started service with a worker thread (HandlerThread) that processed each onHandleIntent(Intent) one after another and stopped itself when the queue was empty. It was deprecated in API 30 because background-start limits made plain services unreliable and because coroutines/WorkManager fit better.

Why it is a problem now. Starting it from the background fails on API 26+; its queue is in memory only (lost on process death unless START_REDELIVER_INTENT via setIntentRedelivery(true)); no constraints, retries or backoff; not lifecycle aware.

Migration under live traffic.

  1. Inventory callers (who starts it, from which context, with which extras).
  2. Replace each task type with a CoroutineWorker (WorkManager) for deferrable, guaranteed work; or with a foreground service for user-visible long work.
  3. Keep serial semantics if needed: WorkManager.beginUniqueWork(name, APPEND, ...) or a Mutex/limitedParallelism(1).
  4. Convert Intent extras to Data (small values, 10 KB limit) and pass IDs, not blobs.
  5. Dual-run: ship the Worker path behind a remote flag; keep the IntentService alive for one release; compare success, latency and crash/ANR numbers.
  6. Remove the service and manifest entry; watch for JobIntentService (also deprecated).
class UploadWorker(ctx: Context, p: WorkerParameters) : CoroutineWorker(ctx, p) {
    override suspend fun doWork(): Result =
        runCatching { upload(inputData.getString("id")!!) }.fold({ Result.success() }, { Result.retry() })
}

Real products. Google's own samples moved from IntentService/JobIntentService to WorkManager; many SDKs (Firebase FirebaseMessagingService replaced GcmListenerService plus IntentService patterns).

Analogy. Changing from a clerk who works through papers on his desk (lost if the office burns down) to a filing system with a tracked ticket for each job.

Common interview traps.

  • Replacing it with a plain thread and losing guaranteed execution.
  • Forgetting that WorkManager is not immediate (use expedited work for urgent tasks).
  • Passing large payloads through WorkManager Data.

notes.title: Foreground service types on Android 14 and 15, and media playback kills
notes.html:
The idea. Android 14 (API 34) made every foreground service declare what kind of work it does, so the system and Google Play can check that it is legitimate.

Rules (API 34 apps targeting 34).

  • Declare android:foregroundServiceType in the manifest and pass the type to startForeground(id, notification, type).
  • Declare the matching permission, for example FOREGROUND_SERVICE_LOCATION, FOREGROUND_SERVICE_MEDIA_PLAYBACK, FOREGROUND_SERVICE_DATA_SYNC, plus the runtime prerequisites (location permission, camera/microphone permission where relevant).
  • Types include camera, connectedDevice, dataSync, health, location, mediaPlayback, mediaProjection, microphone, phoneCall, remoteMessaging, shortService, specialUse, systemExempted (Android 14 added health, remoteMessaging, shortService, specialUse, systemExempted; mediaProcessing arrived in Android 15).
  • A missing type or permission throws SecurityException / MissingForegroundServiceTypeException; wrong prerequisites (e.g. location type with no location permission granted) also throw.
  • shortService is limited to roughly 3 minutes and must call stopSelf(); specialUse requires a justification property and Play review.

Android 15 (API 35) changes (confirm in docs): dataSync and mediaProcessing types get a timeout of about 6 hours per 24 hours; when hit, Service.onTimeout(startId, fgsType) is called and you have a few seconds to stop, or the app crashes with RemoteServiceException. BOOT_COMPLETED receivers can no longer start some FGS types (dataSync, camera, mediaPlayback, phoneCall, mediaProjection, microphone). mediaProjection needs an active user consent token.

Media playback killed at scale (production incident). A music service dies when the user locks the phone for an hour on some OEMs, or after a Play Store listing review fails because the service type was wrong. Checks: correct mediaPlayback type, a MediaSession-linked notification (use MediaStyle/media3 MediaSessionService, which handles foreground logic), audio focus handling, a partial wake lock/WifiLock for streaming (via setWakeMode), battery optimisation guidance, and reading ApplicationExitInfo to see whether kills are REASON_LOW_MEMORY or user/OEM. Using media3 MediaSessionService takes care of foreground start/stop on playback state changes.

Real products. Spotify, JioSaavn, Gaana, YouTube Music; Android Auto only discovers sessions from properly declared services.

Analogy. Android 14 asks for a work permit with your job title written on it; Android 15 adds a time-card limit for some jobs.

Common interview traps.

  • Using dataSync for something that never ends (hits the Android 15 timeout).
  • Forgetting the type-specific permission in the manifest.
  • Assuming one generic type works for everything; Play policy rejects mismatched types.

notes.title: Process priority effect of services
notes.html:
The idea. A service's state directly sets how safe your process is from being killed.

Service state Process class (typical) Kill order
Foreground service Foreground / perceptible, protected very late
Bound by a visible/foreground client At least that client's importance follows client
Started background service Service (A list, B list if old) before foreground, after cached
Started but running a long time (> ~30 min) Demoted to the B-services list earlier
Stopped / unbound Cached first

Details: services started in the background run in "service A" until they have run for a while; the system keeps an LRU. A long-running background service is a poor guarantee. The bound-priority rule means a bound service that serves a visible Activity is as important as that Activity.

Real products. Spotify's service jumps to perceptible when playing; a to-do app's plain service gets killed within minutes in the background.

Analogy. Staff with a red badge (foreground) are never asked to leave first; yellow badge (bound to a VIP) borrow the VIP's rank; no badge goes first.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing started services are protected forever.
  • Forgetting that unbinding drops priority immediately.
  • Using START_STICKY as the only "keep alive" approach.

notes.title: Service versus WorkManager, and the ambiguous "run in background" requirement
notes.html:
The idea. Pick the tool by the contract you need, not by habit.

Need Tool
Deferrable work that must eventually finish, survive reboot, respect constraints (network, charging), retries WorkManager
Immediate work that user started and watches (upload, navigation, music, call) Foreground service (right type)
Short deferred task within seconds from FCM Expedited WorkManager
Exact time (alarm clock, calendar) AlarmManager exact alarms (permission needed)
Server push FCM
Cross-component API for clients Bound service

Ambiguous requirement ("keep syncing in the background"). Ask: does the user know it's running? Does it need to be immediate, or can it run within 15 minutes? What if the network is down? What if the phone is rebooted? How long does it take? Answers map: user-visible continuous = foreground service; periodic and tolerant = PeriodicWorkRequest (minimum 15 minutes); one-off but must complete = OneTime Work with constraints; real-time chat = FCM plus a short expedited job.

Real products. Google Photos backups (WorkManager + FGS when active), Gmail sync (SyncAdapter/WorkManager plus FCM), Uber navigation (foreground service).

Analogy. Courier choices: a motorbike you watch the whole way (foreground service), or a parcel locker that delivers sometime today even if you're asleep (WorkManager).

Common interview traps.

  • Recommending a service for anything "in the background".
  • Forgetting WorkManager has a 15 minute minimum for periodic work.
  • Starting a foreground service for a task that could be deferred (policy and battery penalty).

notes.title: Swipe from recents, stopWithTask and restart backoff
notes.html:
The idea. When a user swipes your app out of the recents screen, the system removes the task and (for most OEMs) kills the process. What happens to your service depends on settings.

  • Default android:stopWithTask="true" (the default): the service is stopped when the task is removed.
  • android:stopWithTask="false": the service keeps running (if the process survives) and onTaskRemoved(rootIntent) is called, where you can persist state or schedule work. If the process is killed and the service is START_STICKY, the system schedules a restart with backoff (~1 s, doubling, up to a limit).
  • The swipe is not a force stop: after force-stop (Settings > Force stop) nothing restarts, including alarms and jobs, until the user launches the app. OEM skins (Xiaomi, Oppo, Vivo, Huawei) treat swipe as force-stop in practice, defeating sticky services.
  • ApplicationExitInfo reports swipe as REASON_USER_REQUESTED on most devices.
override fun onTaskRemoved(rootIntent: Intent?) {
    saveSession()                         // persist; do not rely on staying alive
    WorkManager.getInstance(this).enqueue(syncRequest)
}

Real products. Music players commonly stop on swipe-away; delivery apps (Swiggy/Zomato partner apps) keep tracking only through a foreground service with notification and handle OEM battery whitelisting guidance.

Analogy. Closing the shop door (task removal) versus demolishing the shop (force stop): sometimes staff can keep working inside after the first, never after the second.

Common interview traps.

  • Assuming START_STICKY always revives after swipe.
  • Not saving state in onTaskRemoved.
  • Confusing swipe-away with force-stop.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Started services run until stopped; bound services live while clients are bound; both must be satisfied to destroy.
  • Services run on the main thread; do work on coroutines or a HandlerThread; AIDL calls arrive on Binder threads.
  • onStartCommand return values decide restart: NOT_STICKY, STICKY (null intent), REDELIVER_INTENT; use stopSelf(startId).
  • Foreground services need a notification, a call to startForeground within about 5 s, and on Android 14 a declared type plus permission; Android 15 adds timeouts for dataSync/mediaProcessing and boot restrictions.
  • Background starts are blocked from API 26 (and foreground starts from the background from API 31) unless exempt.
  • IntentService is deprecated: migrate to WorkManager, coroutines, or a foreground service.
  • Service state sets process priority; choose service vs WorkManager vs alarm by the guarantee you need.
  • Swipe-away, force-stop and OEM killers make "always alive" impossible; persist state and design for restart.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between a started service, a bound service, and a service that is both? How does each one stop?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you understand that "who keeps the service alive" is a reference-counting question, which drives leaks, premature kills, and lifecycle callbacks.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A started service is created by startService() and lives until someone calls stopSelf() or stopService(). A bound service is created by bindService() and lives only while at least one client is bound. A service can be both: it stays alive until it has been explicitly stopped AND all clients have unbound. I think of it as two independent reasons to stay alive, and the system destroys the service only when both reasons are gone.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A Service is a component with no UI. The system tracks two things per service record in ActiveServices (inside system_server): a "started" flag (set by startService, cleared by stop) and a set of client connections (added by bindService, removed by unbindService or client death).

startService()  -> onCreate (if new) -> onStartCommand(intent, flags, startId)
bindService()   -> onCreate (if new) -> onBind(intent)   [first client only]
                                      -> later clients get the cached IBinder, no new onBind
unbindService() last client          -> onUnbind(intent)  -> (if not started) onDestroy
stopSelf()/stopService()             -> (if no bound clients) onDestroy

Key rules:

  • onBind is called once per distinct Intent filter-equality (Intent.filterEquals) when the first client binds; the returned IBinder is cached and handed to later clients.
  • onStartCommand is called every startService call, even if the service exists.
  • If started AND bound, stopSelf() does nothing visible until the last client unbinds, and unbinding everyone does nothing while the started flag is set.
  • onUnbind() returning true makes the next bind call onRebind() instead of onBind().
  • bindService with BIND_AUTO_CREATE creates the service if it is not running; without it, bind succeeds only if already running.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class SyncService : Service() {
    private val binder = LocalBinder()
    inner class LocalBinder : Binder() { fun get(): SyncService = this@SyncService }

    override fun onBind(intent: Intent): IBinder = binder
    override fun onStartCommand(intent: Intent?, flags: Int, startId: Int): Int {
        // started path
        return START_NOT_STICKY
    }
}
// Client
bindService(Intent(this, SyncService::class.java), conn, Context.BIND_AUTO_CREATE)
// Later, in matching teardown callback:
unbindService(conn)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking stopSelf() kills a service that still has bound clients. It does not.
  • Binding in onCreate and unbinding in onDestroy of an Activity: the Activity may be stopped for a long time while the connection keeps the service (and its process priority) alive. Pair onStart/onStop.
  • Forgetting that the same service can be started by a background component that is no longer allowed to start it (see Q159).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When is onBind called if three activities bind? → Once, for the first client; others receive the cached IBinder (same Intent filter-equality).
  2. Can a Service be bound from a BroadcastReceiver? → No: bindService throws ReceiverCallNotAllowedException from a manifest receiver context. Use startService/startForegroundService or a peekService pattern.
  3. How does a service die if a bound client's process crashes? → The binder driver notifies system_server (client death), the connection is removed, and if no one else is bound and it is not started, the service is destroyed.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "started runs in background, bound is for client-server." Senior: explains the two independent keep-alive reasons, the cached IBinder, onRebind, and that connections also determine process priority (bound by a foreground client raises the service process).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "download manager" service that was both started and bound by a screen. The team called stopSelf() after the last download but the screen's connection leaked, so the service (and a 60 MB process) stayed until cached-process eviction.

questions.promptHtml: On which thread do Service callbacks run? Is a Service a background thread? When do you still need your own thread or coroutine inside a Service?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The single most common junior misconception. A wrong answer leads to ANRs in Services.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A Service is not a thread and not a separate process by default. Its callbacks (onCreate, onStartCommand, onBind, onDestroy) run on the main thread of the app process. If I do disk or network work there, I block the UI and can hit a Service ANR. So I dispatch work to a coroutine scope, executor, or HandlerThread owned by the service and cancel it in onDestroy.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
ActivityThread receives Service lifecycle transactions over Binder and posts them to the main Looper (the H handler). So service callbacks queue behind UI frames and input. Platform timeouts for Service execution (measured by AMS, not by the Looper):

  • onCreate/onStartCommand/onBind: ~20 s if the process is in the foreground, ~200 s for background services (AOSP ActiveServices.SERVICE_TIMEOUT / SERVICE_BACKGROUND_TIMEOUT). Exceeding it produces "Executing service" ANR.
  • Foreground start: must call startForeground within ~5 s of startForegroundService (Q155).

A Service gains you one thing: process priority and lifecycle tracking by the OS. It gives you no concurrency. android:process=":remote" puts it in another process, but still on that process's main thread.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class UploadService : Service() {
    private val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.IO)

    override fun onStartCommand(intent: Intent?, flags: Int, startId: Int): Int {
        scope.launch {
            try { upload(intent) } finally { stopSelf(startId) }
        }
        return START_NOT_STICKY
    }
    override fun onDestroy() { scope.cancel() }
    override fun onBind(i: Intent?): IBinder? = null
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thread { ... }.start() with no cancel: the work outlives the Service and keeps running in a process the OS will now kill anytime.
  • Calling stopSelf() before the async work finishes (service destroyed, process lowered to cached, work dies).
  • Using GlobalScope.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would you serialize work items? → A single-thread executor or a Channel consumed by one coroutine; stop with stopSelf(startId) after the last item.
  2. Does android:process make it multi-threaded? → No, only a different process; main-thread semantics still apply there.
  3. What replaced IntentService's worker thread model? → See Q160.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE knows "main thread." Senior adds the AMS timeouts, ties the work's lifetime to the service via a scope cancelled in onDestroy, and notes work survives only as long as the process does.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A sync Service doing a 1 MB JSON parse in onStartCommand showed up as 0.3% ANR on low-end devices; moving it to Dispatchers.Default removed it.

questions.promptHtml: Explain START_STICKY, START_NOT_STICKY, START_REDELIVER_INTENT and START_STICKY_COMPATIBILITY. What does each do when the process is killed, and what should I do with the flags argument?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests understanding of what the OS promises after process death, and whether you handle the null-Intent restart.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The return value tells the system what to do if it kills my service process while it is still "started". START_NOT_STICKY: do not recreate it. START_STICKY: recreate it and call onStartCommand with a null Intent. START_REDELIVER_INTENT: recreate it and redeliver the last Intent (retrying pending ones). My service must therefore treat a null Intent as a valid input under START_STICKY.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Return After kill (service still marked started) Intent on restart Typical use
START_NOT_STICKY Not restarted until next explicit start n/a One-shot work you can re-trigger (upload with WorkManager backup)
START_STICKY Recreated, onStartCommand called null Long-running state machine that rebuilds its own state (e.g. media player)
START_REDELIVER_INTENT Recreated Last delivered Intent(s) not yet stopSelf(startId)'d Work whose parameters are in the Intent (download of URL X)
START_STICKY_COMPATIBILITY Legacy: may not be restarted after onStartCommand returns Compat Effectively never used

flags: START_FLAG_REDELIVERY means this is a redelivery after the service was killed (only with REDELIVER). START_FLAG_RETRY means the previous onStartCommand attempt did not return before the process was killed (or the service was restarted after sticky) and the system is retrying. Restart is performed by AMS after a backoff delay (starts around one second and grows for repeated failures; constants live in ActiveServices, verify on current AOSP). On API 26+, a killed service of an app that is now in the background may be restarted only when background-start rules allow it; do not assume instant recovery. Restart also depends on the process being killed by the LMK or OS, not by the user swiping the app away in Settings > Force stop (force stop clears started state entirely).

Kill by startId: with REDELIVER, the system tracks each delivered start request until stopSelf(startId) acknowledges it.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
override fun onStartCommand(intent: Intent?, flags: Int, startId: Int): Int {
    val url = intent?.getStringExtra(EXTRA_URL)
    if (url == null) {            // sticky restart: recover from persisted state
        scope.launch { resumeFromDb(startId) }
    } else {
        scope.launch { download(url); stopSelf(startId) }
    }
    return START_REDELIVER_INTENT
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• intent.getStringExtra(...) without ?. on a START_STICKY service: NullPointerException loop after every OS kill.
  • Using START_STICKY for finite tasks; the service gets resurrected with no work and sits idle consuming priority.
  • Assuming sticky survives the user force-stopping the app (it does not).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does stopSelf(startId) do versus stopSelf()? → Stops only if startId was the most recent start request; otherwise no-op, preventing a race with newer requests.
  2. Does START_STICKY restart on crash? → Yes, a crash is a process death; AMS applies restart-with-backoff and, after repeated crashes, may stop restarting (crash-loop protection).
  3. How do you test it? → adb shell am kill <pkg> while backgrounded (kills a non-foreground process) then watch logs; also "Don't keep activities" does not kill services.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE recites the names. Senior chooses based on state recovery (persisted queue vs Intent parameters), handles null Intents, uses startId correctly, and knows background-start rules can block the restart.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A sticky upload service crashed every restart with NPE on the null Intent, producing a boot-loop of restarts that drained battery until Crashlytics showed 40k crashes/day.

questions.promptHtml: What are the ways a started service can stop, and what is the difference between stopSelf(), stopSelf(startId), and stopService()? When does onDestroy run?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks understanding of lifecycle ownership and race conditions when multiple start requests overlap.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The service can stop itself with stopSelf() or stopSelf(startId), or any component can call stopService(intent). stopSelf(startId) stops only if no newer start request has arrived, which makes it safe when work is queued. The service is destroyed only when it is not started and has no bound clients; then onDestroy runs on the main thread, and I cancel my scope there.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Each startService call increments a startId handed to onStartCommand. stopSelf(startId) asks AMS to stop only if startId equals the last one delivered. This avoids this race: start A (id 1), start B (id 2), A finishes and calls stopSelf() -> B's work is destroyed. With stopSelf(1) it is ignored because id 2 is newer.

Destruction triggers:

  • Last stopSelf/stopService and no clients bound.
  • Last client unbinds and the service was never started (or was stopped).
  • The process dies (no onDestroy is called).
  • Foreground services: also stopForeground(STOP_FOREGROUND_REMOVE) only detaches the notification; the service is still running as a background service until stopped.

onDestroy is not guaranteed on process death, so do not rely on it to persist state.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
scope.launch {
    process(intent)
    stopSelf(startId)            // not stopSelf()
}
// From a component:
context.stopService(Intent(context, UploadService::class.java))

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling stopSelf() at the end of every worker: the second worker is killed by the first.
  • Stopping a foreground service without removing the notification or the FGS state (stopForeground) before stopSelf.
  • Expecting stopService to work for a bound service; it only clears the started flag.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if stopService() is called while a client is bound? → Service keeps running until the last unbind, then onDestroy.
  2. How do you track multiple tasks? → Counter or Channel; call stopSelf(lastStartId) when the queue drains, or stop only when the counter hits zero.
  3. What does a stuck stopForeground(false) cause? → The notification stays dismissible but the service is no longer foreground; process priority drops and the OS may kill it.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "call stopSelf." Senior: explains startId race, does cleanup in onDestroy knowing it is not guaranteed, and persists progress independently.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An image-sync service stopped itself after the first batch while a second batch was queued, causing "missing photos" bug reports at 2% of users until stopSelf(startId) was adopted.

questions.promptHtml: What is a foreground service, why does it require a notification, and what is the "5 second rule" for startForegroundService()? What happens if I violate it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: FGS are the most heavily regulated area of Android; incorrect usage causes crashes and Play policy rejections.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A foreground service tells the OS "the user is aware of and benefits from this ongoing work", so the process gets higher priority and is far less likely to be killed. In exchange it must show an ongoing notification. Since API 26 I start it with startForegroundService() from the allowed contexts, and I must call startForeground() within about five seconds of the Service starting, otherwise the app crashes with ForegroundServiceDidNotStartInTimeException (and on older releases an ANR-style RemoteServiceException).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Contract: Context.startForegroundService(intent) -> service created -> onStartCommand -> startForeground(id, notification[, type]). The 5 s is the documented budget; AMS arms a timer when startForegroundService is called and clears it when startForeground is called. If it fires, the process is asked to crash with RemoteServiceException (API 26-30) or ForegroundServiceDidNotStartInTimeException (API 31+). Do not rely on any slack: the platform constant has varied by release.
  • Calling startForegroundService then stopSelf() before startForeground: crash. Even when you decide there is no work, you must call startForeground first.
  • Notification: must be posted on a channel; if the channel is invalid or the notification small icon missing, the call fails. API 33+: the user can dismiss the FGS notification (except some types); the service keeps running. API 31+: notification display may be deferred ~10 s unless setForegroundServiceBehavior(FOREGROUND_SERVICE_IMMEDIATE) or an exempt type (see Q170).
  • Manifest: FOREGROUND_SERVICE permission (normal permission) since API 28. For targetSdk 34+, also a foregroundServiceType and matching permission (Q161).
  • Starting from the background: restricted since Android 12 (Q159/Q162).
startForegroundService()  --5s timer armed-->  onCreate -> onStartCommand
                                                    |
                                      startForeground(id, n, type)  --> timer cleared

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class TrackingService : Service() {
    override fun onStartCommand(intent: Intent?, flags: Int, startId: Int): Int {
        val n = NotificationCompat.Builder(this, "tracking")
            .setSmallIcon(R.drawable.ic_stat)
            .setContentTitle("Tracking active")
            .setOngoing(true)
            .build()
        ServiceCompat.startForeground(
            this, 1, n, ServiceInfo.FOREGROUND_SERVICE_TYPE_LOCATION
        )
        // then do work; if nothing to do, still reached startForeground first
        return START_NOT_STICKY
    }
    override fun onBind(i: Intent?): IBinder? = null
}
// Caller:
ContextCompat.startForegroundService(ctx, Intent(ctx, TrackingService::class.java))

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Doing heavy work (DI graph init, reading a database) before startForeground and missing the deadline on slow devices.
  • Early stopSelf() in a branch before startForeground.
  • Using the Activity-bound startService() path then promoting later; fine only if the app is in the foreground.
  • Missing notification channel creation on API 26+.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does startForeground require POST_NOTIFICATIONS on API 33? → Service still becomes foreground, but the notification is hidden if permission is denied; it still appears in the Task Manager.
  2. startService() vs startForegroundService() from the foreground? → startService() from a visible app is allowed; you can then call startForeground() later. From the background (API 26+), you must use startForegroundService() and hit the 5 s rule.
  3. How do you stop a foreground service cleanly? → stopForeground(STOP_FOREGROUND_REMOVE) then stopSelf().

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "needs a notification." Senior: explains the AMS timer, early-stop crash, deferred notification, dismissibility on 13+, type declaration on 14+, and that a FGS is not a license to run forever (15 timeouts, Play policy).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "sync now" FGS crashed with ForegroundServiceDidNotStartInTimeException on 0.8% of devices because Hilt and Room were initialised before startForeground; moving the notification before everything else fixed it.

questions.contextHtml:
A messaging app has ChatSyncService, started when the app backgrounds. In production Crashlytics shows a fatal NullPointerException at ChatSyncService.onStartCommand for ~12k crashes/day, only on devices with <3 GB RAM, mostly right after the user returns from other apps. Code:

class ChatSyncService : Service() {
    private lateinit var userId: String

    override fun onStartCommand(intent: Intent, flags: Int, startId: Int): Int {
        userId = intent.getStringExtra("uid")!!
        CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO).launch {
            sync(userId)
            stopSelf()
        }
        return START_STICKY
    }
    override fun onBind(i: Intent?): IBinder? = null
}

Stack: java.lang.NullPointerException: Parameter specified as non-null is null: ... parameter intent. Red herring: the team suspects a race in sync() because crashes cluster near a recent sync refactor.
questions.promptHtml: What is the bug, why does it only happen on low-RAM devices, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a null check on uid" or "make sync thread-safe." Misses that the Intent parameter itself is null on sticky restart, and that the exposure correlates with process kills, not with sync logic.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the crash happen at app foreground or on a cold OS restart? (restart signals null Intent). Which devices and what is the kill frequency? (low RAM = more LMK). Is the service meant to survive kills or be re-triggered? (decides sticky vs not).
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix: declare intent: Intent? and return early with stopSelf(startId); return START_NOT_STICKY when null. Ship via staged rollout. Crashes stop immediately.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) null Intent from START_STICKY restart after LMK; (b) null uid extra from a caller bug; (c) race in sync; (d) Kotlin intrinsics check after a refactor changed the nullability.
  4. How I'd verify each: The message says "parameter intent", not uid -> (a). Reproduce: adb shell am start ..., background app, adb shell am kill com.app, observe restart in adb logcat -b events | grep am_proc. Check the Java override in decompiled bytecode: platform passes null on sticky restart.
  5. Root cause: START_STICKY restarts the service after process death and calls onStartCommand(null, flags, startId). The Kotlin override declares non-null Intent, so the compiler-generated parameter check throws. Low-RAM devices die more often, so they hit it more.
  6. Fix: Short-term: nullable Intent + guard. Long-term: persist the user id in storage (DataStore/Room) so a sticky restart can recover; or use START_NOT_STICKY and re-enqueue via WorkManager; use stopSelf(startId); own a scope cancelled in onDestroy.
override fun onStartCommand(intent: Intent?, flags: Int, startId: Int): Int {
    val uid = intent?.getStringExtra("uid") ?: session.currentUserId()
    if (uid == null) { stopSelf(startId); return START_NOT_STICKY }
    scope.launch { sync(uid); stopSelf(startId) }
    return START_NOT_STICKY
}
  1. Prevention: Lint (the platform signature is nullable; a Intent non-null override is a code-review smell), instrumented test using am kill, ban !! on Intent extras in services, chaos testing with LMK simulation.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not just wrap in try/catch (the restart loop continues). I would not keep START_STICKY for a finite sync: it resurrects empty services. Dropping sticky means a kill mid-sync is dropped; I accept that and back it with a periodic job.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the product wants the sync to resume exactly after a kill? → Persist a cursor; use START_REDELIVER_INTENT or a WorkManager chain; both need idempotent sync.
  • Why does the crash not reproduce with "Don't keep activities"? → That option destroys Activities, not service processes.
  • Could AMS crash-loop protection hide this? → It limits restart frequency but does not prevent the first crash; the crashes keep counting.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite from a chat client: a "harmless" refactor made a service Intent non-null via IDE conversion. Crashes tracked LMK pressure, not code paths, so the team chased the wrong module for two days until someone read the exception text.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Adds ?. on extras or blames threading.
  • Hire: Identifies null Intent on sticky restart, fixes signature, picks the right return value.
  • Strong hire: Also persists state, tests with am kill, explains low-RAM correlation, and questions whether the service should be sticky at all.

questions.promptHtml: How do you implement a bound service for same-process clients using Binder? What are the lifecycle rules for binding and unbinding from an Activity, and what are the leak risks?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Binding is the standard way UI talks to a long-lived component (music, location); sloppy binding leaks ServiceConnection and Activities.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The service returns a Binder subclass from onBind that exposes itself (or an interface). The client calls bindService(intent, conn, BIND_AUTO_CREATE) and gets the IBinder in onServiceConnected. I bind in onStart, unbind in onStop, and never keep the service reference past unbind. Leaks come from forgetting unbindService or holding the service reference in a static or ViewModel.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• For same-process clients onServiceConnected receives the actual Binder object (no marshalling); for another process you get a proxy.
  • bindService is asynchronous: the binder arrives later on the main thread. Do not use the service right after the call.
  • ServiceConnection callbacks: onServiceConnected, onServiceDisconnected (the service process crashed or was killed; the binding stays and reconnects when the service restarts), onBindingDied (API 28+, binding is dead and must be re-requested), onNullBinding (API 28+, onBind returned null).
  • bindService returns false if the service cannot be found or the binding is not permitted. Per the Context docs, call unbindService regardless of the return value to release the connection; unbinding a connection that was never passed to bindService throws IllegalArgumentException: Service not registered.
  • Bind with the Activity's context for a binding tied to that Activity's lifetime. Binding with applicationContext outlives the Activity, so do it only when the binding should be application-scoped, and own it from an application-scoped class.
  • Flags: BIND_AUTO_CREATE (create service if needed), BIND_ABOVE_CLIENT, BIND_IMPORTANT (client's importance transfers), BIND_NOT_FOREGROUND.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class PlayerService : Service() {
    inner class LocalBinder : Binder() { val service get() = this@PlayerService }
    private val binder = LocalBinder()
    override fun onBind(intent: Intent): IBinder = binder
}

class PlayerActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    private var player: PlayerService? = null
    private var bound = false
    private val conn = object : ServiceConnection {
        override fun onServiceConnected(n: ComponentName, b: IBinder) {
            player = (b as PlayerService.LocalBinder).service; bound = true
        }
        override fun onServiceDisconnected(n: ComponentName) { player = null }
    }
    override fun onStart() {
        super.onStart()
        bindService(Intent(this, PlayerService::class.java), conn, BIND_AUTO_CREATE)
        bound = true   // unbind even if bindService returned false
    }
    override fun onStop() {
        if (bound) { unbindService(conn); bound = false; player = null }
        super.onStop()
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Binding in onCreate, unbinding in onDestroy: the connection is held while the Activity is stopped and not visible; the log line Activity has leaked ServiceConnection appears if never unbound.
  • Casting IBinder to the local type for a service in another process (ClassCastException).
  • Passing the connection out of the Activity into a singleton.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is onServiceDisconnected not called on unbindService? → It is only called on unexpected loss (process death).
  2. How would a ViewModel hold the binder? → Store the interface, not the Activity; bind with applicationContext and unbind in onCleared, or expose through a repository.
  3. What does BIND_AUTO_CREATE do to process priority? → The service process is ranked at least as high as the binding client (see Q164).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE can write the boilerplate. Senior pairs bind/unbind with onStart/onStop, handles disconnect/binding-died, and keeps UI state in a ViewModel with service access behind an interface.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A music app bound in onCreate and, after navigation changes, retained 7 Activity instances through un-unbound connections; LeakCanary showed ServiceConnectionLeaked-style retention.

questions.subtopic: Messenger vs AIDL vs local Binder
questions.promptHtml: How do you choose between a local Binder, a Messenger, and AIDL for talking to a service? What threading and safety differences matter?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests IPC choice with a threading model. (Binder internals are chunk 14, so keep this at service-API level.)

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: If the client and service are in the same process, I use a local Binder (or better, an interface). For cross-process one-way message passing I use a Messenger: it serialises calls on a Handler thread, so no thread-safety worries. For cross-process request/response with typed methods and concurrency I use AIDL, where calls arrive on Binder pool threads and I must make my service thread-safe.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Local Binder Messenger AIDL
Process Same Cross Cross (also works same)
Thread of callee Caller's thread (direct call) Handler's thread (one at a time) Binder pool thread (up to 16, parallel)
API shape Plain Kotlin Message with what/Bundle Generated interface, Parcelable args
Replies Return values Via replyTo Messenger Return values or callbacks
Type safety Full None (what + bundle) Compile-time

Cross-process notes: service must be exported="true" if other apps bind it, and you should protect it with a signature permission. Since Android 11, an app binding another app's service needs <queries> for package visibility. All data is marshalled into a Parcel, subject to the ~1 MB shared transaction buffer (see the IPC chunk). oneway AIDL methods do not block the caller and are delivered serially per binder object.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Messenger service
class EchoService : Service() {
    private val handler = object : Handler(Looper.getMainLooper()) {
        override fun handleMessage(msg: Message) {
            msg.replyTo?.send(Message.obtain(null, 2, msg.arg1 + 1, 0))
        }
    }
    private val messenger = Messenger(handler)
    override fun onBind(i: Intent): IBinder = messenger.binder
}
// IStats.aidl
interface IStats { int count(); oneway void ping(); }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Treating AIDL service state as single-threaded and getting races under concurrent calls.
  • Using Messenger for large payloads (it is still Binder).
  • Exposing an exported service without permission checks (Binder.getCallingUid()).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where does a Messenger's Handler run? → On the Looper you passed; main by default, which means you can ANR your service, so use a HandlerThread.
  2. How do you secure an AIDL service? → Signature-level custom permission, checkCallingPermission, validate inputs.
  3. What if the service process dies mid-call? → The caller gets DeadObjectException; handle via linkToDeath or onBindingDied.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "AIDL is for IPC." Senior chooses by thread model and failure modes, and avoids IPC entirely when a same-process interface suffices.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An SDK team exposed an AIDL service with unsynchronised state; two host apps calling at once corrupted a counter. Switching to a single-threaded Messenger cut the bug and the cost was latency of 2-3 ms, acceptable.

questions.promptHtml: What changed in Android 8.0 for starting services from the background, what counts as "background", and what are the legitimate ways to start work from there?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The foundational policy behind most FGS and WorkManager decisions; explains IllegalStateException: Not allowed to start service.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: From API 26, an app that is in the background cannot call startService() and gets IllegalStateException ("app is in background"). It can call startForegroundService() and must call startForeground() within about five seconds. An app counts as foreground if it has a visible activity, a foreground service, or is bound by a foreground app. After the app moves to the background, there is a short grace window (a few minutes) before restrictions apply. Legit alternatives: WorkManager/JobScheduler, high-priority FCM, alarms, bound services, or user-visible FGS.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Background = no visible component, not in a foreground service, not bound by a foreground process. Bound services remain allowed to bind.
  • Idle: after the grace period the system stops the app's background services as if stopSelf() was called (running services get onDestroy).
  • Temporary allowlist: high-priority FCM message, PendingIntent sent by the system (notification action, widget click), SmsManager result broadcasts, and JobScheduler jobs give a short window (documented in the 8.0 behavior-changes page; typically a few minutes/short). Use these as exemption, not as a design.
  • Android 8 also limited implicit broadcasts for manifest receivers (S2 chunk).
  • Android 12 (API 31) tightened it further for foreground services: even startForegroundService() from the background throws ForegroundServiceStartNotAllowedException unless an exemption applies (Q162).
  • Android 9 (API 28) added the FOREGROUND_SERVICE permission requirement.
App visible / FGS / bound by FG   --> startService OK
App background (post grace)       --> startService: IllegalStateException
                                      startForegroundService: OK on 8-11, restricted on 12+

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Good: let the platform wake you
val req = OneTimeWorkRequestBuilder<SyncWorker>()
    .setExpedited(OutOfQuotaPolicy.RUN_AS_NON_EXPEDITED_WORK_REQUEST)
    .build()
WorkManager.getInstance(ctx).enqueue(req)

// Bad: from a plain background callback
ctx.startService(Intent(ctx, SyncService::class.java))  // may throw IllegalStateException

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Catching IllegalStateException and ignoring it: work silently never happens.
  • Treating a bound service as exempt from kill: it is still a background process.
  • Testing only on emulators with the app in the foreground.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is it targetSdk-dependent? → The 8.0 background limits apply to apps targeting 26+, and system-wide limits for older targets apply when the user opts in; since modern targets are far above 26, treat it as universal (verify for your supported range).
  2. What gives a legit temporary exemption? → High-priority FCM, notification-action PendingIntent, visible activity, bound by FG app.
  3. How do you debug "why was I considered background"? → adb shell dumpsys activity services <pkg> and dumpsys activity processes, plus logcat ActivityManager lines.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "use JobScheduler." Senior explains the definition of background, the exemptions, the 12+ tightening, and designs flows so work starts from a legal context.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A fitness app lost "morning sync" after upgrading targetSdk; the old code started a service from a broadcast receiver on a timer, which began failing on 8+ devices at 4% of users.

questions.promptHtml: IntentService is deprecated. What did it do, why was it deprecated, and what do you use instead?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks awareness of the modern replacement and why the model no longer fits Android 8+.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: IntentService was a Service that ran each Intent sequentially on a worker HandlerThread and stopped itself when the queue drained. It was deprecated in API 30 (it still exists; it was not removed) because it is a background service, which Android 8+ blocks, and WorkManager/coroutines supersede it. I use WorkManager for deferrable guaranteed work, a coroutine in a foreground service for ongoing user-visible work, or a plain coroutine in the app process for short in-process tasks.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
IntentService: onHandleIntent(Intent) on a worker thread; serial queue; auto stopSelf(startId). Problems: (1) background service restrictions cause it to be stopped or not started in background; (2) not persistent across reboots; (3) no constraints, retries, or backoff; (4) JobIntentService was its compatibility bridge and is also deprecated in favour of WorkManager.

Replacement table:

Need Replacement
Deferrable, must eventually run, survive reboot WorkManager (CoroutineWorker)
Immediate user-initiated, ongoing Foreground service
Short in-process, tied to app lifetime Coroutine in an app scope
Exact time AlarmManager with exact permission, then start from allowed context

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class UploadWorker(ctx: Context, p: WorkerParameters) : CoroutineWorker(ctx, p) {
    override suspend fun doWork(): Result {
        val path = inputData.getString("path") ?: return Result.failure()
        return try { upload(path); Result.success() } catch (e: IOException) { Result.retry() }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Replacing IntentService by a plain Service + thread and hitting the same background limits.
  • Using JobIntentService in new code.
  • Assuming WorkManager runs "immediately": it is deferrable unless expedited.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you keep serial ordering? → Unique work with ExistingWorkPolicy.APPEND_OR_REPLACE or chained work (details are the WorkManager chunk).
  2. Is IntentService removed from the SDK? → No; deprecated since API 30 but present.
  3. When would an FGS beat WorkManager? → When the user expects immediate, visible, ongoing work (navigation, call, playback).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "use WorkManager." Senior maps each former IntentService use to a category, states what is guaranteed, and notes that expedited work has quotas.
