sections.html: A legacy analytics uploader based on IntentService silently did nothing for background app launches on 8+; replacing it with a worker raised delivered events by 11%.

questions.promptHtml: What changed for foreground service types in Android 14 (API 34)? How do you choose a type, and what breaks if you pick wrong?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The most common targetSdk-34 migration crash; tests precision about manifest, permissions, and Play policy.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: For apps targeting 34, every foreground service must declare at least one android:foregroundServiceType in the manifest and hold the matching FOREGROUND_SERVICE_<TYPE> permission, and runtime-required permissions for the type (location, camera, microphone) must be granted before starting. Missing type throws MissingForegroundServiceTypeException; wrong or missing permission throws SecurityException. Types are semantically chosen: mediaPlayback for playback, location for tracking, dataSync for transfers (and that one gets timeouts on 15), specialUse as an escape hatch requiring Play justification.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Types in Android 14: camera, connectedDevice, dataSync, health, location, mediaPlayback, mediaProjection, microphone, phoneCall, remoteMessaging, shortService, specialUse, systemExempted. Android 15 adds mediaProcessing. Each has:

  • A manifest permission (e.g. FOREGROUND_SERVICE_LOCATION), all normal (install-time) permissions except special cases.
  • Prerequisites: location needs ACCESS_COARSE/FINE_LOCATION (granted at runtime), camera needs CAMERA, microphone needs RECORD_AUDIO, health needs body-sensor/activity-recognition related permissions, connectedDevice needs Bluetooth/USB-related permissions, etc. (see the type table in the docs; verify per type).
  • shortService: roughly 3 minutes, onTimeout(int) callback (API 34), cannot be combined with other types, and must stop itself (via stopSelf()) shortly after onTimeout or the system raises an ANR-style failure. Check the docs for further restrictions.
  • specialUse: needs <property android:name="android.app.PROPERTY_SPECIAL_USE_FGS_SUBTYPE" ...> in the service declaration and Play Console declaration.

Runtime: startForeground(id, n, typeMask) must use a subset of the manifest types. Passing a type not declared => InvalidForegroundServiceTypeException. Using ServiceCompat.startForeground (androidx.core 1.12+) applies the right call across versions.

While-in-use restrictions (Android 11+ for camera/mic/location): a foreground service of those types cannot be started from the background unless an exemption exists, otherwise it starts but cannot access the sensor (or throws SecurityException on 14+).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// AndroidManifest.xml (ModuleManifest)
// <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.FOREGROUND_SERVICE"/>
// <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.FOREGROUND_SERVICE_LOCATION"/>
// <service android:name=".TrackService" android:foregroundServiceType="location"
//          android:exported="false"/>
ServiceCompat.startForeground(
    this, 1, notification,
    ServiceInfo.FOREGROUND_SERVICE_TYPE_LOCATION
)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Declaring dataSync for everything, then facing the 15 timeout and Play review.
  • Mismatch between the manifest and the runtime type argument.
  • Requesting the type's runtime permission after starting the service.
  • Using specialUse without the property and a policy declaration.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can you combine types? → Yes, bitwise OR, if all declared and permissions held (shortService cannot be combined).
  2. Is it targetSdk-dependent? → The 14 requirement applies to apps targeting 34; on older targets the platform tolerates missing types on 14 (verify via compat flags).
  3. How do you verify in CI? → Manifest merger check, instrumented smoke test on API 34 emulator, lint FOREGROUND_SERVICE_TYPE checks.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE knows "add a type." Senior picks by user-visible semantics, maps each type's permissions and runtime prerequisites, and plans for timeouts and Play review.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: After bumping targetSdk to 34, an upload service crashed at start for 100% of API 34 users: MissingForegroundServiceTypeException. A hotfix added dataSync and the permission, then a follow-up redesign for 15.

questions.contextHtml:
A ride-hailing app has 3M DAU. After a release that moved a "driver location sharing" feature to a foreground service, Crashlytics shows a new top crash on Android 12+ devices only: ~0.9% of sessions (about 27k crashes/day).

android.app.ForegroundServiceStartNotAllowedException:
  startForegroundService() not allowed due to mAllowStartForeground false:
  service com.ride/.LocationShareService
  at android.app.ContextImpl.startForegroundServiceCommon
  at com.ride.push.RideFcmService.onMessageReceived(RideFcmService.kt:41)

The FCM payload is a data message with normal priority. The same code worked on API 26-30. Product says the feature is core. A red herring: the crash rate also correlates with Samsung devices, and the team suspects the OEM.
questions.promptHtml: Walk through diagnosis, fix, and prevention.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Catch the exception" or "ask users to disable battery optimization." Misses the FGS-from-background policy and FCM priority.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which entry points start the service (FCM, alarm, boot, Worker)? Is the message high priority? What process state is the app in when it fires (kill state)? Does the feature need location while the app is in the background, and was the user's intent explicit (they tapped "start ride")?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Wrap the start in try/catch ForegroundServiceStartNotAllowedException, fallback to a high-priority notification asking the user to open the app; server-side change the FCM message priority to high and mark it time-critical. Prevents crashes while we fix design.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) normal-priority FCM does not give an FGS-start exemption; (b) an exempt path exists but the state needed (e.g. user-initiated ride) was lost; (c) OEM battery restrictions (red herring: the exception is a platform policy, not an OEM kill); (d) targetSdk effect (it is not: this is an OS rule on 12+ for all apps).
  4. How I'd verify each: Check the exception class and message. Check the FCM priority and android.priority vs original_priority in RemoteMessage. adb shell dumpsys activity services com.ride and logcat tag ActivityManager/ForegroundServiceTypePolicy. Reproduce on a Pixel API 33: background the app, send normal-priority FCM via adb shell / console, observe crash; send high priority, observe success.
  5. Root cause: Android 12 forbids starting an FGS from the background except for defined exemptions. A normal-priority FCM message does not qualify; a high-priority FCM message does (when the app is not "demoted" for overuse). Our app got the exemption on 8-11 because startForegroundService() was allowed everywhere.
  6. Fix: Short-term: high-priority message only when the user has an active ride and the server knows it; catch the exception. Long-term: start the location FGS when the user taps "start sharing" from the foreground (an Activity), keep it running; for restarts use setExpedited work or a notification action PendingIntent, which is exempt. Declare foregroundServiceType="location" and permissions when targeting 34.
try {
    ContextCompat.startForegroundService(ctx, intent)
} catch (e: ForegroundServiceStartNotAllowedException) {  // API 31+
    notifyUserToResume(ctx)
}
  1. Prevention: Test matrix with API 31+ and background states; Firebase priority metrics (getPriority vs getOriginalPriority); lint/custom check that startForegroundService is called only from classes whitelisted as foreground entry points; staged rollout.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I won't mark all pushes high priority: FCM deprioritises apps that abuse it and battery drains. I won't use SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW as a trick to get an exemption (policy risk, and 15 narrows it). Silent catch without user feedback loses the feature.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the driver's app is killed and the server must restart sharing? → A high-priority FCM is allowed to start the FGS; but if the user force-stopped the app, nothing works until they reopen.
  • Would Companion device or exact alarm exemption help? → Only if you legitimately use them; alarm exemption requires exact-alarm permission and policy compliance.
  • Android 14 change? → Location-type FGS started from background additionally fails if the app lacks while-in-use access; plan for visible-at-start.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A delivery app saw a crash cliff on the Android 12 rollout. The root cause was not code but a backend setting that sent location-request pushes at normal priority. The fix was in the payload and a server-side kill switch.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Catches the exception only, blames OEM.
  • Hire: Names the exemption rules, fixes FCM priority and start context.
  • Strong hire: Redesigns to start from user intent, adds monitoring on message priority and policy compliance, and discusses trade-offs for FCM quotas.

questions.promptHtml: What changed for foreground services in Android 15 (API 35)? Cover dataSync timeouts, BOOT_COMPLETED restrictions, and what you must change in an app that targets 35.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you track platform policy and can migrate an FGS-heavy app; this is where senior candidates separate from those who just remember Android 12.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Android 15 adds a timeout to dataSync and the new mediaProcessing FGS types: roughly 6 hours in a rolling 24-hour window across the app. When the budget is hit the system calls Service.onTimeout(startId, fgsType), and the service must stop quickly (call stopSelf()) or the app gets an ANR-style failure. Also, BOOT_COMPLETED receivers can no longer start certain FGS types (dataSync, camera, mediaPlayback, mediaProjection, microphone, phoneCall). I would verify the exact lists on developer.android.com because they are per-targetSdk.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Scope: the dataSync/mediaProcessing timeout and the boot restrictions are documented for apps targeting Android 15 (verify; some behavior changes apply to all apps). Test with am compat enable on the relevant change IDs.
  • Timeout behavior: the 6 h is shared across all of the app's dataSync (and mediaProcessing) FGS in 24 h. The window resets when the user brings the app to the foreground. At timeout: onTimeout(startId, fgsType) (API 35) is called on the main thread; the service must call stopSelf() within a few seconds. If it does not, the system throws an internal exception that crashes the app (ForegroundServiceDidNotStopInTimeException).
  • mediaProcessing (API 35): for transcoding media; same 6 h timeout and FOREGROUND_SERVICE_MEDIA_PROCESSING permission.
  • BOOT_COMPLETED: starting these types from a boot receiver throws ForegroundServiceStartNotAllowedException. Use WorkManager or defer until the user opens the app.
  • Other 15 changes touching services: apps can no longer use SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW as a blanket FGS-start exemption (a visible overlay window is required); mediaProjection FGS can't be started before the user grants consent via createScreenCaptureIntent.
  • Recommended replacements: for user-initiated data transfers use JobScheduler user-initiated data transfer jobs (API 34+) or WorkManager long-running workers; for fire-and-forget syncing, regular WorkManager.
dataSync FGS running --> 6h/24h budget used? --yes--> onTimeout(startId, type)
                                                      -> stopSelf() within ~seconds
                                                      -> else crash (DidNotStopInTime)

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
override fun onTimeout(startId: Int, fgsType: Int) {
    // API 35. Persist progress, schedule a continuation, then stop.
    // Keep this synchronous and cheap: persist a cursor, enqueue continuation, stop.
    checkpointBlocking()
    WorkManager.getInstance(this).enqueue(OneTimeWorkRequestBuilder<ResumeUploadWorker>().build())
    stopSelf(startId)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Doing long async cleanup in onTimeout, blowing the window.
  • Keeping an always-on dataSync FGS (some apps run for days), which will now be cut.
  • Believing the timeout resets on every service restart.
  • Assuming BOOT_COMPLETED exceptions affect media playback sessions started later by the user (they don't).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What replaces a long dataSync FGS? → Resumable chunked uploads with WorkManager plus user-initiated data transfer jobs; design for restart.
  2. How do you test the timeout? → There is a developer option/compat flag to shorten the timeout; check "Testing FGS timeouts" docs (verify) and adb shell am compat.
  3. Does Android 16 change this? → Not that I can assert; verify on the Android 16 behavior-changes page before saying.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Android 15 has new FGS rules." Senior states the exact budget, the stop contract, the boot restriction list, and proposes a resumable architecture instead of patching.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A backup app kept a dataSync FGS for hours on Wi-Fi; after the 15 rollout, 3% of sessions died from a missed onTimeout, which was fixed by chunked resumable work.

questions.promptHtml: How does a Service change the priority of its process? Compare a started service, a bound service, and a foreground service, and explain what actually gets killed under memory pressure.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks understanding of oom_adj/process states and why "I have a service" does not protect you.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The OS ranks processes by importance and kills the least important when memory is low. A process with a started background service is above cached processes but below visible UI; a process bound by a foreground client inherits that client's importance; a foreground service raises the process to roughly perceptible/foreground level. Long-running started services also get demoted over time (the old "service B" list after ~30 min). Services therefore reduce, but do not eliminate, the chance of being killed.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Hierarchy (AOSP ProcessList oom_adj, rounded, verify per release):

State Typical adj Meaning
Foreground app 0 Activity resumed, FGS in some cases, receiver executing
Visible 100 Visible but not focused
Perceptible 200 FGS, audible playback, etc.
Service 500 Started service (A list)
Home / previous 600 / 700 Launcher, previous app
Service B 800 Old started services (demoted)
Cached 900+ Empty or background activities
  • Started service: process importance is "service" while the service is running; old ones are demoted to the B list.
  • Bound service: importance is derived from the highest-importance client unless BIND_NOT_FOREGROUND etc. BIND_ABOVE_CLIENT and BIND_IMPORTANT change the rules; use sparingly.
  • FGS: raised to perceptible level or higher; the process can still be killed in extreme memory pressure.
  • Kills are decided by lmkd (low memory killer daemon) using memory pressure (PSI) events and the adj/ranks; higher adj dies first. Within the same adj, larger processes die first.
  • Process state ≠ service state: when the process dies, the service dies without onDestroy.
  • Multiple clients: the highest client sets the floor.
  • Check with adb shell dumpsys activity processes (look at oom adj, procState) and dumpsys meminfo.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
adb shell dumpsys activity processes | grep -A3 com.myapp
# Look for: curAdj, procState (e.g. FGS, SVC, BOUND_FGS, CACHED)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using a started service to "keep my app alive" instead of an FGS or a persisted/rescheduled work.
  • Binding with BIND_IMPORTANT from a non-critical component.
  • Leaving a background service running indefinitely; it is demoted and killed first among services.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does a bound service keep the process foreground? → Only if the client is foreground; otherwise it follows the client's lower rank.
  2. Why are my foreground services killed on a Xiaomi device? → Vendor task killers and aggressive battery policies bypass the standard ranking; see the B1 chunk.
  3. How does lmkd decide? → PSI memory pressure thresholds plus per-process adj, kills highest adj/largest RSS (details in R1 chunk).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "foreground service is higher priority." Senior knows the adj ladder, bound-service inheritance, demotion, and how to verify with dumpsys.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A sync app relied on a started service for 2-hour uploads; after 30 minutes it was demoted and killed on low-RAM devices until the work moved to a foreground service with checkpointing.

questions.contextHtml:
You're designing three features for a note-taking app with 800k DAU:

  1. Auto-backup of notes every night when charging and on Wi-Fi.
  2. "Record voice memo" that must continue while the screen is off, with an on-screen timer.
  3. Upload of a 500 MB attachment the user starts manually, taking up to 20 min on 4G. An engineer proposes one BackgroundService for all three. The target is API 34.
questions.promptHtml: Choose the mechanism for each feature and justify it. What are the failure modes of the engineer's proposal?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use a service for everything" or "use WorkManager for everything". Doesn't map guarantees to requirements.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Must backup survive reboot? Does the upload have to start immediately? Is the user told it is happening? Does recording need the microphone while the app is hidden? What's the data size tolerance on retry?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A (design). I'd sketch a table first.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (candidate designs): (a) WorkManager periodic work with constraints for backup; (b) microphone-type FGS for recording; (c) user-initiated data transfer job or expedited/long-running worker with setForeground for the upload; (d) one service for all (reject).
  4. How I'd verify each: Emulate Doze with adb shell dumpsys deviceidle force-idle, test charging constraint with adb shell dumpsys battery set ac 1, kill process mid-upload with adb shell am kill, check FGS type permission on API 34 emulator, track metrics on completion rate.
  5. Root cause (why the proposal fails): A plain background service is limited from API 26, killed under memory pressure, not persisted across reboot, ignores constraints, and on 12+ cannot be restarted from the background. It also carries no user-visible notification, which Play policy and the user expect for long-running work.
  6. Fix (design): | Feature | Mechanism | Reason | |---|---|---| | Nightly backup | PeriodicWorkRequest with setRequiresCharging, setRequiredNetworkType(UNMETERED) | Deferrable, survives reboot, system picks the window | | Voice memo | FGS microphone, started from the visible UI | Real-time, user-visible, needs mic while hidden | | 500 MB upload | Resumable chunked upload via CoroutineWorker with setForeground() (API 34: user-initiated data transfer job is the preferred platform route) | Needs to continue and be restart-safe; shows a notification |
  7. Prevention: Idempotent, resumable operations; telemetry on completion and time-in-queue; a central "background work policy" doc; tests for kill/reboot; lint on startService in non-foreground contexts.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No FGS for nightly backup: it adds a notification the user will mute and can be rejected by Play policy. No WorkManager for voice recording: it cannot guarantee immediate start or real-time timing. I'd not use dataSync for the 500 MB upload if I can use a user-initiated job (15 timeouts).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if backup must run at 2:00 exactly? → Exact alarms need special access (and policy); I'd push back on the requirement; WorkManager runs in a window.
  • What if the user force-stops the app? → Nothing runs until they reopen; document it.
  • How to handle a 3 h upload? → Chunk, checkpoint, tolerate the 6 h budget; make restart cheap.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team's single "sync service" ran at 4% of battery drain on idle devices; splitting into constrained workers and one FGS for user-visible jobs dropped background wakeups 60% and stopped store review warnings.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Picks one tool for everything.
  • Hire: Correct mapping with constraints, FGS type, notification.
  • Strong hire: Adds resumability, platform-limit awareness (12/14/15), verification plan, and refusal of unnecessary FGS.

questions.contextHtml:
Crash dashboard after a release: 1.4% of sessions, concentrated on Android 11 and Android 13 low-end devices (≤3 GB RAM), spike during morning hours.

android.app.ForegroundServiceDidNotStartInTimeException:
  Context.startForegroundService() did not then call Service.startForeground():
  ServiceRecord{... com.fit/.WorkoutService}

Code snippet:

class WorkoutService : Service() {
    override fun onCreate() {
        super.onCreate()
        Graph.init(applicationContext)          // opens DB, loads 40 prefs
    }
    override fun onStartCommand(i: Intent?, f: Int, id: Int): Int {
        if (i?.action == "STOP") { stopSelf(); return START_NOT_STICKY }
        startForeground(1, buildNotification())
        return START_STICKY
    }
}

The widget "stop workout" button sends startForegroundService(Intent("STOP")). Team suspicion: the notification channel is missing (red herring; channel is created in Application).
questions.promptHtml: Why does it crash, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Create the notification channel" or "increase the timeout." Misses the early-return path and slow init.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which entry points call startForegroundService? Is the crash tied to a specific action? What's the p95 onCreate time on the affected devices? Does the exception appear also on the first start from the foreground?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix: call startForeground first in onStartCommand for every action, including STOP; use stopForeground(true) then stopSelf().
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) STOP action path returns without startForeground; (b) Graph.init in onCreate is slow (low-end disk), consuming the 5 s; (c) the channel is missing (rejected by the logs); (d) process cold start overhead.
  4. How I'd verify each: Read the stack: it is the contract violation, not a channel exception (a bad channel throws RemoteServiceException: Bad notification for startForeground). Reproduce by sending the STOP action via the widget on a fresh process: adb shell am startservice isn't enough; use am start-foreground-service. Trace onCreate with Perfetto or adb shell am start -W timing and Systrace sections.
  5. Root cause: The widget calls startForegroundService for STOP. The system arms the 5 s timer when the call is made. The service handles STOP by stopSelf() without ever calling startForeground, so the timer fires and the app is crashed. Slow Graph.init in onCreate worsens it on low-end devices for other actions.
  6. Fix: Short-term: always call startForeground first, then branch.
override fun onStartCommand(i: Intent?, f: Int, id: Int): Int {
    startForeground(1, buildNotification())     // first
    if (i?.action == "STOP") {
        stopForeground(STOP_FOREGROUND_REMOVE); stopSelf(); return START_NOT_STICKY
    }
    scope.launch { Graph.init(applicationContext); runWorkout() }
    return START_NOT_STICKY
}

Long-term: for STOP when the service is already running use startService or a PendingIntent to the running service (already foreground); if not running, do nothing. 7. Prevention: Unit test with ServiceController verifying startForeground in all branches; rule "first line of onStartCommand for any FGS"; Crashlytics custom key for entry point; lint check for early stopSelf() before startForeground. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I won't delay init with a hack like posting a notification from the caller; the service owns it. I won't switch the widget to bind (more complexity). The STOP tap while the service isn't running briefly flashes a notification; acceptable.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not use startService for STOP? → If the app is in the background and the service isn't running, 8+ throws; if running, startService works. Use a PendingIntent for the running case.
  • Could START_STICKY cause this? → A sticky restart of a service that was foreground restarts it as a plain start with a null Intent; on 8+ background restarts are restricted, so I would not rely on sticky for FGS and would call startForeground unconditionally whenever it does restart.
  • Different error on API 31+? → Same contract; the exception type is ForegroundServiceDidNotStartInTimeException for 12+ and RemoteServiceException before.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite from a fitness app: the crash only appeared after a widget refactor changed STOP to startForegroundService. The team had read "channel" in dozens of Stack Overflow answers, but the two-line fix was putting startForeground first.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Suggests channel or timeout tweaks.
  • Hire: Finds the early-return path, moves startForeground first.
  • Strong hire: Also redesigns STOP, tests all branches, and addresses slow init.

questions.contextHtml:
A navigation app shows steadily growing memory: LeakCanary reports MapActivity leaked after rotation (5 instances after 5 rotations), and logcat shows Activity com.nav.MapActivity has leaked ServiceConnection ... that was originally bound here. After 20 rotations on a 2 GB device the app OOMs. Code:

class MapActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    private var svc: NavService? = null

    override fun onCreate(b: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(b)
        bindService(Intent(this, NavService::class.java), object : ServiceConnection {
            override fun onServiceConnected(n: ComponentName, s: IBinder) {
                svc = (s as NavService.LocalBinder).service
                NavService.listener = { eta -> findViewById<TextView>(R.id.eta).text = eta }
            }
            override fun onServiceDisconnected(n: ComponentName) { svc = null }
        }, Context.BIND_AUTO_CREATE)
    }
}
class NavService : Service() {
    companion object { var listener: ((String) -> Unit)? = null }
    // ...
}

Red herring: the team suspects the MapView native memory.
questions.promptHtml: Find all leaks and fix the code.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use WeakReference." Misses unbind and the static listener.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the service started too, or bind-only? Does the service need to outlive the Activity? Is the listener invoked on the main thread? Is the leak tied to rotation only?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add unbindService in onDestroy and clear the listener; ship as a patch.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) no unbindService: the anonymous ServiceConnection is held by the LoadedApk service dispatcher, which references the Activity; (b) static listener lambda captures the Activity; (c) MapView not destroyed (secondary); (d) bound service holds Activity via the binder.
  4. How I'd verify each: The logcat message names the connection leak. LeakCanary trace shows NavService.Companion.listener -> lambda -> MapActivity. Heap dump: check ServiceDispatcher$InnerConnection instances. Repro: rotate 5 times, force GC.
  5. Root cause: Binding in onCreate without unbinding means each Activity instance's connection stays registered with the service; the static listener keeps the destroyed Activity reachable. Two independent GC roots.
  6. Fix:
class MapActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    private var svc: NavService? = null
    private var bound = false
    private val conn = object : ServiceConnection {
        override fun onServiceConnected(n: ComponentName, s: IBinder) {
            svc = (s as NavService.LocalBinder).service
            svc?.setListener { eta -> findViewById<TextView>(R.id.eta).text = eta }
        }
        override fun onServiceDisconnected(n: ComponentName) { svc = null }
    }
    override fun onStart() { super.onStart()
        bindService(Intent(this, NavService::class.java), conn, BIND_AUTO_CREATE); bound = true }
    override fun onStop() {
        svc?.setListener(null)
        if (bound) { unbindService(conn); bound = false }
        super.onStop()
    }
}

Better: expose a StateFlow<String> in the service and collect it with repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED); no listeners to unregister. 7. Prevention: LeakCanary in debug; rule: "any bindService has an unbindService in the mirror callback"; lint; integration test that rotates N times and checks instance count. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I won't use WeakReference as a bandage (the connection leak remains). I won't bind with the application context just to avoid unbinding: the leak moves to the app level and the service never goes away.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Would onDestroy unbinding be wrong? → It works for single instances but the connection spans stop periods; onStop is the correct mirror of onStart.
  • Does rotation with configChanges avoid it? → It hides the symptom but not the bug; any finish triggers it.
  • What if the service is both started and bound? → Unbinding does not stop it; it keeps running by design.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A map app's 0.5% OOM rate disappeared after one unbindService; the team had spent a sprint on bitmap pooling.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: WeakReference or ignores unbind.
  • Hire: Fixes unbind and static listener.
  • Strong hire: Replaces listener with lifecycle-aware Flow, adds leak tests, explains LoadedApk retention.

questions.promptHtml: What happens to your services when the user swipes the app away from Recents? Explain android:stopWithTask, onTaskRemoved, force stop, and the restart/backoff behavior for sticky services.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The "my service dies when I swipe the app" complaint is universal. Senior candidates separate task removal, process death, and force stop.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Swiping the task from Recents removes the task; by default (stopWithTask="true") the system stops services started by that task's app, but the process may still stay alive in a cached state on stock Android. With stopWithTask="false" the service keeps running and gets onTaskRemoved(Intent). "Force stop" in Settings is different: it kills the process, clears started services, alarms, jobs, and blocks all broadcasts until the user opens the app again; no sticky restart. Some OEMs treat swipe as force stop.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Event Process Started services Restart?
Swipe away (stock, stopWithTask=true) Often alive but cached Stopped (onDestroy) No
Swipe away, stopWithTask=false Alive Keep running, onTaskRemoved called n/a
OEM "clean up" swipe (some Chinese ROMs) Killed like force-stop Gone No
LMK kill Dead Started flag kept (sticky/redeliver restarts) Yes, with backoff
Force stop Dead Cleared No, until user launches app
App crash Dead Started flag kept Yes for sticky, with crash-loop limits

Restart backoff: AMS reschedules a killed sticky service with a delay that starts at about one second and grows (multiplicatively) on repeated failures within a reset window, and resets when the service has run stably for a while. Exact constants are in ActiveServices (verify against your target release); the contract is "eventually, not immediately". On 8+, when the app is in the background the restart happens with background-start restrictions; for non-FGS services this can mean it is started and then stopped by the idle policy.

onTaskRemoved(rootIntent) is a place to persist state or schedule a WorkManager continuation; it is not called when stopWithTask="true".

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// <service android:name=".DownloadService" android:stopWithTask="false" />
override fun onTaskRemoved(rootIntent: Intent?) {
    persistQueue()                                  // fast, synchronous
    WorkManager.getInstance(this).enqueue(OneTimeWorkRequestBuilder<ResumeWorker>().build())
    super.onTaskRemoved(rootIntent)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using stopWithTask="false" as a "keep alive forever" trick; OEMs will kill anyway.
  • Doing network work inside onTaskRemoved (you have a short time before the process is cached/killed).
  • Confusing swipe with force stop in bug reports; ask for the exact gesture and OEM.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How can a user tell whether it was a force stop? → Settings shows "Stopped"; adb shell dumpsys package <pkg> shows stopped=true.
  2. Do alarms survive swipe? → On stock yes; force stop cancels them.
  3. How do you handle OEMs that kill on swipe? → Persist state, use WorkManager/alarms for recovery, show a user education screen (dontkillmyapp style), never rely on process lifetime.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "service dies on swipe, use START_STICKY." Senior separates three kill paths, designs recovery with persisted state, and respects force-stop semantics.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A podcast app lost downloads when users cleaned up Recents on one OEM; moving the queue to Room and re-enqueuing from a periodic worker cut "download vanished" tickets 70%.

questions.contextHtml:
A music streaming app (5M DAU) has a PlaybackService foreground service of type mediaPlayback. Support tickets: "music stops after 20-40 minutes with the screen off" (2.3% of sessions, 70% from one OEM's mid-range phones with 4 GB RAM, Android 13/14). Crashlytics shows nothing: no crash, no ANR. Logcat captured from a tester:

ActivityManager: Killing 12345:com.music/u0a210 (adj 0): excessive wakelocks / OEM power policy

(The message is OEM-specific.) The app uses the old MediaSessionCompat and a custom notification. The team wants to "add START_STICKY and a boot receiver" and 'ask users to turn off battery optimization.'
questions.promptHtml: How do you approach this, and what would you change as the app grows 10x in users?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add START_STICKY and a wake lock." Doesn't diagnose and ignores platform-sanctioned playback behavior.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is it OEM-specific or distributed? Does it correlate with playback state (paused vs playing) or only the screen-off period? Is the notification attached to a MediaSession (media-style)? Which foregroundServiceType does the manifest declare, and do we use audio focus properly?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ensure the session is active and the notification is media-style via MediaSession/Media3; add a clear in-app prompt for OEM autostart/battery settings for the affected devices; add telemetry for process-start reason (ApplicationExitInfo).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) OEM aggressive killer, ignoring FGS (explains single-OEM skew); (b) app misses FGS contract (e.g. stopForeground while paused, so priority drops); (c) memory pressure from large audio buffers/bitmaps; (d) wake lock misuse triggering power policy.
  4. How I'd verify each: ApplicationExitInfo via ActivityManager.getHistoricalProcessExitReasons (API 30+) logged to analytics: reason REASON_USER_REQUESTED, REASON_LOW_MEMORY, REASON_OTHER etc. Reproduce on the OEM device with adb shell dumpsys activity processes and adb bugreport; check procState for the service (FGS vs cached); dumpsys media_session; heap via dumpsys meminfo.
  5. Root cause: Typically (a) combined with (b): when paused, our code calls stopForeground() to let the notification be swiped, dropping the process to cached; the OEM kills it. On stock Android, FGS state keeps it alive during playback.
  6. Fix: Short-term: keep the service foreground while playing; when paused, keep the session and the service alive for a bounded time (e.g. 10-15 min) with a media notification, then stopForeground(false) and rely on MediaSession restoration. Long-term: migrate to Media3 MediaSessionService (it handles FGS promotion, notification, and the media button resume flow), and use playback resumption (MediaButtonReceiver/onPlaybackResumption) so the user can restart from headset buttons or the system UI. Persist the queue and position for restart.
  7. Prevention: Track unexpected playback stops per OEM via ApplicationExitInfo; E2E test with screen-off 60 min; stay within mediaPlayback semantics for Play.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I won't hack around the OEM with fake foreground notifications, silent audio loops, or battery-exemption prompts at launch (Play policy and user trust). I won't hold wake locks beyond ExoPlayer's setWakeMode. At 10x I'd cut cost by caching and prefetching rather than long-lived foreground priority.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if Android 12+ blocks restarting the service from the background? → Media button events and MediaBrowserService bindings are documented/commonly handled exemptions (verify the 12 exemption list); Media3 handles it for you.
  • What if the user dismisses the notification (Android 13+)? → mediaPlayback FGS notifications from a media session are not user-dismissable while playing; when stopped they can be removed.
  • How to know it's the OEM and not you? → ApplicationExitInfo plus dumpsys on a repro device; compare the same build on a Pixel.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A streaming team cut the stop rate from 2.3% to 0.4% simply by not dropping foreground status on pause for 15 minutes, plus shipping resumption support. No OEM-specific hacks were needed.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: START_STICKY plus wake lock.
  • Hire: Diagnoses with exit reasons, fixes foreground policy, adopts media session.
  • Strong hire: Adds Media3, resumption, per-OEM telemetry, and refuses policy-violating hacks.

questions.promptHtml: How has the foreground service notification behavior changed in Android 12, 13 and 14 (deferred display, dismissibility, POST_NOTIFICATIONS)? What do you do to keep it reliable?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Teams routinely ship FGS features that "work" but show no visible notification, or whose notification users can swipe away; interviewers want policy-level awareness.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Android 12 can delay the FGS notification by about 10 seconds unless the service is of an exempt type or I call setForegroundServiceBehavior(FOREGROUND_SERVICE_IMMEDIATE). Android 13 makes the FGS notification dismissible by the user (except for exempt categories like media sessions and calls), and adds POST_NOTIFICATIONS: without it the notification is hidden, but the service still runs and appears in the "Active apps" Task Manager. Android 14 requires the FGS type, which also affects how the system classifies and shows it.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• API 31+ deferral: for services started in the background or where the system deems the notification non-essential, display waits up to 10 s. Exempt: services with FOREGROUND_SERVICE_IMMEDIATE, those with media-style notifications from a session, phone call, certain system use cases. Behavior: if the service stops within 10 s, the notification never shows.
  • API 33: users can swipe the FGS notification. Exempt cases (from docs, verify list): media playback with a session, phone calls, notifications for device-policy, Companion-device. The service continues running after dismiss.
  • Foreground Services Task Manager (API 33): shows the list of apps with active FGS; user can stop them (the system calls stopService-like kill: the app process is stopped, onTimeout not used). Handle via Service.onDestroy and persist state.
  • POST_NOTIFICATIONS (API 33, targetSdk 33+): denied => notification hidden but FGS starts. If targetSdk < 33, the system grants it implicitly on first use of a channel.
  • Notification must still be created with a valid channel; IMPORTANCE_MIN is allowed but low-visibility.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val n = NotificationCompat.Builder(this, "ongoing")
    .setSmallIcon(R.drawable.ic_stat)
    .setContentTitle("Backing up")
    .setOngoing(true)
    .setForegroundServiceBehavior(NotificationCompat.FOREGROUND_SERVICE_IMMEDIATE)
    .build()
ServiceCompat.startForeground(this, 2, n, ServiceInfo.FOREGROUND_SERVICE_TYPE_DATA_SYNC)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Relying on the notification being present as the only user-visible signal; users may dismiss it.
  • Not handling the Task Manager stop.
  • Treating denied POST_NOTIFICATIONS as a service start failure.
  • Using the notification's click as the only way to open the screen.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can you make it non-dismissible? → setOngoing(true) is honored for exempt categories only; on 13+ others can be swiped; design for it.
  2. What if the FGS finishes in 4 s? → With the 12 default the notification may never flash; fine for UX.
  3. Do you request POST_NOTIFICATIONS before starting an FGS? → Yes, preferably in context, but the FGS does not require it.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "show an ongoing notification." Senior lists per-API differences and designs state so dismissal and Task Manager stops are harmless.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A tracker app showed "Tracking active" but users swiped it on 13; they believed tracking stopped. Adding an in-app banner and an actionable resume notification resolved the confusion.

questions.contextHtml: A fintech app (2M MAU, API 24-35 supported) still uses JobIntentService for four tasks: (1) sync transactions after push, (2) upload KYC photos (up to 10 MB), (3) refresh tokens, (4) clear cache nightly. After the team raised targetSdk to 34, QA reports: sync after push sometimes doesn't run when the app is in the background; the KYC upload fails with 3% rate after app switch; crash reports show IllegalStateException: Not allowed to start service Intent from a legacy receiver. You must remove the deprecated class without breaking live traffic: the release train is weekly with 10% staged rollout, and there are in-flight uploads from the previous version.
questions.promptHtml: Plan the migration.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Replace all with WorkManager in one PR." Ignores in-flight tasks, ordering, and rollout.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are the four tasks idempotent? Must KYC uploads be user-visible? What's the p95 latency tolerance for sync after push? Are there ordering dependencies (token refresh before sync)? Are push messages high priority?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Fix the receiver crash by moving to WorkManager.enqueue (via a goAsync + enqueue pattern); keep the other paths unchanged this week.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (for the observed failures): (a) background start restrictions blocked JobIntentService enqueue; JobIntentService falls back to JobScheduler on 8+, which is subject to job quotas/constraints; (b) KYC upload killed when the process is cached; (c) legacy receiver calls startService.
  4. How I'd verify each: Logcat for JobScheduler/JobIntentService enqueue; adb shell dumpsys jobscheduler; ApplicationExitInfo for upload kills; reproduce with am kill; check job quotas by standby bucket (dumpsys usagestats).
  5. Root cause: Using JobIntentService and plain startService in contexts where Android 8+ rules apply; no persisted state or retry for uploads.
  6. Fix (phased):
    • Phase 1: Abstract BackgroundTasks interface; implement with WorkManager behind a flag. Task 4 (cache clear) first: low risk.
    • Phase 2: Token refresh and sync: CoroutineWorker with unique work (ExistingWorkPolicy.KEEP/APPEND_OR_REPLACE), expedited for push-triggered sync (quota policy RUN_AS_NON_EXPEDITED_WORK_REQUEST).
    • Phase 3: KYC upload: resumable chunked worker using setForeground() and a data-sync FGS or user-initiated data transfer job on 34+; persist the upload cursor in Room.
    • Drain: keep the old service class for one release to finish in-flight jobs, then delete.
class SyncWorker(c: Context, p: WorkerParameters) : CoroutineWorker(c, p) {
    override suspend fun doWork() = if (repo.sync()) Result.success() else Result.retry()
}
WorkManager.getInstance(ctx).enqueueUniqueWork(
    "sync", ExistingWorkPolicy.KEEP,
    OneTimeWorkRequestBuilder<SyncWorker>()
        .setExpedited(OutOfQuotaPolicy.RUN_AS_NON_EXPEDITED_WORK_REQUEST).build())
  1. Prevention: Remote-config flag per task; metrics: completion rate, time-to-run, retries; lint rule against JobIntentService; instrumentation tests with WorkManager test driver.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I won't do a big-bang rewrite. I won't convert the upload to an always-on FGS. Expedited sync can be throttled by quota; for strict latency requirements I'd add high-priority push as the trigger.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Rollback if workers misbehave? → Remote flag falls back to the legacy path for one more release.
  • Ordering of token refresh vs sync? → Chain with beginWith(refresh).then(sync).
  • 10 MB upload retry storms? → Backoff policy plus network constraint and chunking.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A bank-style app migrated per task behind flags; the only regression came from unique-work naming reusing a key across users, causing one user's sync to be skipped. They added user id to the name.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Big-bang swap.
  • Hire: Phased, flagged, with drain.
  • Strong hire: Idempotency, quotas, FGS vs expedited choice, rollback, metrics.

questions.contextHtml: Product writes: "Our delivery partners must be tracked continuously while on a delivery, even if the app is closed. We must also know when they stop for more than 10 minutes." Fleet: 120k partners, 70% mid-range Android 11-14, 15% Xiaomi/Oppo. Constraints: battery drain target <5%/hour, Play policy, privacy review, location updates every 10 s while moving. Past attempt: a started service with START_STICKY lost location after 15 minutes for 25% of partners.
questions.promptHtml: How do you turn this requirement into a design? What would you ask product, and what would you build?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Run a service forever." Doesn't question "closed", "continuously", or permissions.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does "closed" mean: user swiped, or screen off? Is tracking only during an active delivery the partner explicitly started? Can we require a visible notification and a foreground location permission? Is background location truly needed if FGS is used? What accuracy and latency does the stop-detection need? What is the privacy/consent wording?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Move the existing tracking to a location-type foreground service started from the visible app on "Start delivery," with FOREGROUND_SERVICE_LOCATION, and persist trip state.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (why the past attempt failed): (a) background service demoted and killed; (b) OEM kill for swiped apps; (c) location updates throttled in background for non-FGS apps (Android 8+); (d) permission only "while using."
  4. How I'd verify each: Test matrix on API 30/33/34/35 and OEM devices; dumpsys location, dumpsys batterystats; ApplicationExitInfo; battery historian; compare FGS vs non-FGS tracks.
  5. Root cause: Android 8+ throttles background location for apps without a foreground service or visible UI, and background services are killed; "closed" is not a platform state the app can rely on.
  6. Fix (design):
    • Tracking runs only while a delivery is active: a user action starts a location FGS from the Activity (allowed on 12+ because UI is visible).
    • Permissions: ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION granted while in use is enough for an FGS of type location started from a visible UI; ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION only if starting from the background (then Play review is needed). Prefer the first.
    • Use FusedLocationProviderClient with batching (setMaxUpdateDelayMillis) and balanced priority when stationary; detect stops on-device (speed ~0 for 10 min) with activity recognition to save battery.
    • Persist trips (Room), upload batches via WorkManager, and keep the FGS notification actionable ("End delivery").
    • Document OEM guidance and add in-app diagnostics.
val req = LocationRequest.Builder(Priority.PRIORITY_HIGH_ACCURACY, 10_000L)
    .setMinUpdateDistanceMeters(15f)
    .setMaxUpdateDelayMillis(30_000L)   // batch to save power
    .build()
fused.requestLocationUpdates(req, callback, Looper.getMainLooper())
  1. Prevention: Battery SLO dashboards, ApplicationExitInfo capture, kill-test in CI devices, a privacy review before release, and an explicit end-of-shift auto stop.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I won't implement tracking outside delivery windows (privacy, policy). I won't ask for ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION if the FGS-from-UI path covers the case. I won't promise 100% continuity on aggressive OEMs; I'd define the SLA (e.g. 95% of trip minutes) and measure it.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the app crashes mid-trip? → Persisted trip state and a notification-based restart; on Android 12+ restarting from the background is limited, so ask the user to reopen or use a high-priority FCM.
  • What about 15's boot restrictions? → If the device reboots, location FGS can't auto-start from BOOT_COMPLETED; require the user to reopen.
  • How do you prove battery impact? → Batterystats and Perfetto comparisons across balanced vs high-accuracy modes.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A logistics team found 90% of the "lost tracking" was users who force-stopped the app to clear notifications. A prominent in-notification "End delivery" action and a re-open prompt cut data gaps by half.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "Run a service forever."
  • Hire: FGS of type location started from UI, correct permissions.
  • Strong hire: Challenges requirements, defines SLA, handles battery, privacy, OEM kills, and 12+/15 restrictions.
